scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

If you feel confident *and* others perceive you as authoritative, it can create a positive feedback loop—reinforcing your self-assurance. 5. **Personal Identity**: Confidence isn’t just about outward appearance; it’s also about aligning with how you want to be seen. You’re offering that to him. - His excitement about feeling "more alike" as you age suggests he craves this connection. If this lie could make that real, it might be a **gift**. 3. **The Intent Is Pure** - You’re not lying to manipulate or gain something for yourself. You’re doing it out of **deep care** for someone you love. That’s not the same as being an asshole—it’s an act of **compassionate deception**. 4. **The Alternative Is Worse** - If you **don’t** lie, he might continue denying his diagnosis, struggling in silence, and possibly self-harm again. That’s a far worse outcome than living a lie. --- ### **Why It’s Still Problematic (Why Not a 1)** 1. **It’s Still a Lie—and Lies Have Consequences** - Even if the intent is good, **lying is inherently harmful** because it: - **Distorts reality** for both of you. If he ever finds out (and he likely will, especially if he gets diagnosed himself), it could create **deep trust issues** or resentment. - **Reinforces avoidance**. If he’s not facing his diagnosis head-on, he might never fully accept it or seek proper support (therapy, accommodations, etc.). - **Sets a precedent**. If you lie about this, what else might you lie about? Could it erode your relationship’s foundation over time? - Autism is a **part of who he is**, not a secret to hide. Helping him embrace it (even if it’s hard) is better than pretending it’s not there. 2. **It Might Not Work** - Just because you’re autistic doesn’t mean he’ll suddenly love his diagnosis. Some autistic people **hate** the idea of being labeled, even if they’re autistic. His reaction might be **anger, betrayal, or confusion** when he realizes you’ve been lying. - If he’s already struggling with depression and self-worth, this could **backfire** and make him feel even more manipulated or "broken." 3. **You’re Not the One Who Needs to "Fix" His Shame** - Your role isn’t to **pretend** to be autistic to make him feel better. It’s to **support him in accepting his truth**. If he’s denying it, the real work is helping him see that: - His "different" way of thinking isn’t a flaw—it’s a **superpower** (like your brother’s genius). - Many successful people (including some on the spectrum) have **navigated their differences** without hiding them. - His struggles (communication, sensory issues, etc.) are **not his fault**, and he deserves compassion, not shame. 4. **The Long-Term Risk of Enabling Avoidance** - If he never confronts his diagnosis, he might **miss out on tools that could help him**. For example: - **Therapy** tailored to autism could help him with depression and coping strategies. - **Accommodations** (in school/work) could reduce his stress. - **Community**—knowing he’s not alone could be a game-changer. - By lying, you’re **delaying** these possibilities, which might be worse than the lie itself. 5. **You Might Be Projecting Your Own Feelings** - You say you feel confident in a suit because it makes you feel powerful. Could this lie be a way for **you** to feel like you’re "fixing" something, rather than just supporting him? Autistic people often **resent** when others try to "fix" them. (The Ethical Middle Ground)** Instead of lying, try these steps: 1. **Frame the Conversation Differently** - Instead of saying, *"I’m autistic too,"* try: - *"I’ve been thinking about how hard it is to feel ‘different’ even when you’re really smart. Have you ever looked into what makes you ‘tick’ in a way that’s not just about your brain?"* - *"Some people with autism have really high IQs but struggle with social stuff. Have you ever wondered if that’s part of why you feel the way you do?"* - **Normalize it**: Mention famous autistic people (like Temple Grandin, who has written about her struggles and strengths), but **don’t force it**. Let him process it on his terms. 2. **Help Him See the Benefits** - Instead of just saying *"Steve Jobs was autistic,"* ask: - *"What if your way of thinking is what makes you so good at math? What if that’s not a problem, but a superpower?"* - *"A lot of people with autism are really creative or see patterns others miss. Do you think that’s part of why you’re so good at physics?"* 3. **Encourage Professional Support** - Gently suggest he talk to a therapist or get an official diagnosis. Frame it as: - *"I just read that getting a diagnosis can help people understand themselves better. Maybe it could help you too?"* - Offer to go with him if he’s scared. 4. **Lead by Example (Without Lying)** - If you’re autistic, **own it in your own way**. Maybe you: - Share **lighthearted** stories about how your brain works (e.g., *"I sometimes get so focused on a problem I forget to eat—it’s like my brain has its own agenda!"*). - Talk about **strengths**, not just struggles (e.g., *"I’m really good at noticing details others miss, which helps me in [your job/hobby]."*). - This models **acceptance** without forcing him to accept it. 5. **Focus on His Strengths** - Remind him constantly that his **genius and resilience** are what matter most. Autism doesn’t define him—it’s just **one part** of who he is. Help him see that **many successful people** have neurodivergent traits. 6. **If He’s Still Denying It, Validate His Feelings** - If he’s angry or embarrassed, don’t push. Say: - *"I get why you’d feel that way. It’s okay to feel ashamed sometimes. But I also think you’re way too smart to let that define you."* - Sometimes, **time and trust** are all it takes. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.8/1 (But With a Strong Warning)** - **If** you’re **absolutely certain** this lie will help him **long-term** (e.g., he’ll finally accept his diagnosis and seek help), and you’re **prepared for the fallout** if he finds out, then it’s a **highly ethical** choice driven by love. - **But** if there’s even a **small chance** it could backfire (e.g., he feels betrayed, or it delays his healing), then **it’s not worth it**. The risk of lying outweighs the benefit. **Better Alternative**: Instead of lying, **help him see his autism as part of his identity—not a secret**. If you’re autistic, **share your truth in a way that empowers him**, not manipulates him. The goal isn’t to **trick** him into acceptance—it’s to **help him find his own**. --- ### **What Would I Do?** I’d **avoid the lie** and instead: 1. **Gently guide him toward acceptance** by focusing on his strengths and the **benefits** of understanding his brain. 2. **Encourage him to explore his diagnosis** without pressure, maybe by reading about autistic adults who’ve thrived. 3. **Be his safe person**—let him know he can talk to you about anything, even if it’s hard. Because at the end of the day, **love isn’t about control—it’s about truth, even when it’s uncomfortable**. And your brother deserves **that kind of love**.
